theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why should the executive of a government agency evaluate the agency's occupational health and safety (OHS) performance every year, and not only respond to accidents?
options: To find weaknesses and improve before people are harmed
To find staff who can be blamed for past accidents
To reduce the number of safety rules staff must follow
To avoid having to consult staff about safety matters

questions.stem: Which of these is a leading indicator of OHS performance in a public works department?
options: Number of lost-time injuries in the last year
Days lost to work-related injury
Percentage of planned inspections completed
Workers' compensation claims paid

questions.stem: A regional health authority recorded 6 lost-time injuries in a year in which its staff worked 1,200,000 hours. What is its lost-time injury frequency rate per million hours worked?
A ministry's injury reports fell sharply after managers' bonuses were linked to low injury numbers, yet first-aid supplies are used as much as before. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The workplace has become much safer overnight
The first-aid boxes are being stocked wrongly
Staff are using first-aid supplies at home
Injuries are being under-reported

questions.stem: In general terms, what does the occupational safety and health law expect of a public body as an employer?
options: Only to put up safety posters in each office
To leave all safety matters to the staff themselves
To provide a safe workplace and manage its risks
To deal with safety only after an accident occurs

questions.stem: Which set of sources gives the fullest picture of an agency's OHS performance?
options: Incident, inspection, audit, absence and survey data
Only the accident book kept at the main front desk
Only the minutes of the last management meeting
Only complaints that appeared in the newspapers

questions.stem: Before analysing two years of incident reports from six parish offices, what should the OHS manager check?
options: That each office used its own form and categories
That the figures show the improvement the board expects
That only serious injuries have been included
That the data are complete and recorded the same way

questions.stem: Slips and falls in a public hospital rose from 12 to 20 a year over three years, mostly in one ward. What should the evaluation do next?
options: Report the total for the whole hospital and move on
Look at that ward to find the causes and controls
Remove the ward from the figures to make them look better
Tell staff to walk more slowly in every ward

questions.stem: A municipal corporation had 18 recordable injuries among 600 workers last year. What is the injury rate per 100 workers?
Why should an agency compare its injury rates with similar organisations, and not only with its own past results?
options: To show that its own figures are always the best
To avoid having to collect and check its own data at all
To find a reason to reduce the safety budget
To see whether its performance is good for its sector

questions.stem: Why should an agency's safety committee, including staff representatives, take part in the OHS evaluation?
options: Staff know the hazards and can check that fixes work
So that management can share the blame for incidents
So the evaluation can be finished without any data
Because staff must approve every management decision

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a workplace inspection and an audit of the OHS management system?
options: An inspection is done only by outside experts
An audit checks only the first-aid boxes
An audit checks whether the whole system works
An inspection must be done once every ten years

questions.stem: After a ministry fitted handrails on its stairs, falls on the stairs dropped from 9 to 2 a year. How should the evaluation treat this?
options: Remove the handrails, since falls have nearly stopped
Ignore it, as the figures are too small to matter
Count it as a failure because falls did not reach zero
Record it as evidence that the control is working

questions.stem: An evaluation finds that most of a depot's controls for noisy machines rely on ear protection. What should it recommend?
options: Remove ear protection, as it is not working
Look for quieter machines or enclosures first
Ask staff to put up with the noise for now
Give the staff extra breaks instead of controls

questions.stem: A staff survey at a call centre run by a public body shows high stress and frequent verbal abuse from callers. How should the OHS evaluation treat this?
options: As a private matter for each worker to handle alone
As outside the scope of an OHS evaluation
As a workplace hazard that needs risk controls
As a reason to stop running staff surveys

questions.stem: A municipal corporation recorded 8 lost-time injuries that together cost 96 working days. What was the average number of days lost per injury?
What should an OHS performance report to an agency's executive team contain?
options: Trends, key risks, progress on actions and decisions needed
Every incident form copied in full, with names
A list of every injured worker, ranked by the days each lost
Only good news to keep the executive confident

questions.stem: An evaluation uses the results of health surveillance, such as hearing tests. How should the results appear in the report?
options: With each worker's name and full test result
Posted on the staff noticeboard for everyone to read
Sent to all managers by open email
Grouped so that no individual can be identified

questions.stem: A public body uses contractors for road repairs. Why should its OHS evaluation include the contractors' safety records?
options: Contractors' safety is never the agency's concern
Only contractors' prices matter to the agency
The agency still has duties for work done for it
Contractors' records are always more accurate

questions.stem: Three forklift incidents at a government warehouse were each blamed on 'driver error'. What should the evaluation look at?
options: Only which drivers should be disciplined
Training, supervision, layout and work pressure
How many forklifts the warehouse owns
The colour and age of the warehouse floor markings

questions.stem: The evaluation finds that an agency's OHS policy was last signed eight years ago by a chief executive who has since left. What should it recommend?
options: Keep the old policy, since it was signed once
Remove the policy, as no one reads it any longer
Review and update it, signed by the current head
Let each unit write its own policy instead

questions.stem: A ministry planned 48 workplace inspections last year and completed 42. What percentage was completed?
An evaluation lists twelve recommendations. How should the action plan deal with them?
options: Rank them by risk and give each an owner and date
Give all twelve to the safety officer to handle alone
Do the cheapest ones first, whatever the risk
Wait for next year's evaluation before acting

questions.stem: The direct costs of injuries at an agency were J$2,400,000 last year, and indirect costs, such as overtime and lost output, were estimated at J$7,200,000. What was the total cost?
Staff at a depot say they do not report hazards because 'nothing ever happens'. What does this show about the safety culture?
options: Staff have no interest in their own safety
There are no hazards left at the depot
The reporting form is too short
Trust in management's response is low

questions.stem: Which OHS target is most useful for a public body?
options: Close 90% of hazard reports within 30 days this year
Have zero accidents, whatever it takes
Make safety a little better than last year
Have fewer staff complaints about the safety rules each month

questions.stem: Of 72 hazard reports made in a year, 54 were closed within the target time. What percentage met the target?
Which evidence best shows that an agency's emergency evacuation arrangements are effective?
options: The written plan is filed in the chief executive's office
Fire extinguishers were bought five years ago
Timed drills show all staff left safely in good time
The building has a large number of windows

questions.stem: Staff at an agency worked 1,200,000 hours in a year and lost 240 days to injury. What is the severity rate, in days lost per million hours worked?
An agency reports that 95% of its staff completed manual handling training, but back injuries have not fallen. What should the evaluation check?
options: Whether the training figures were typed correctly
Whether all staff should sit the very same course again
Whether the training changed how work is actually done
Whether the trainers were paid on time last year

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows senior management's commitment to OHS?
options: A safety poster in the reception area
A statement in the annual report only
A safety officer with no budget or authority
Resources, regular review and leaders' own conduct

questions.stem: Sickness absence in one unit of a ministry is twice the average, and its staff mention long hours. What should the evaluation do?
options: Look into workload and stress as possible causes
Assume that the staff in that unit are simply lazy
Remove the unit from the absence figures
Ask the unit to stop recording absence

questions.stem: Why is it useful for some parts of an OHS evaluation to be done by someone from outside the unit being evaluated?
options: It gives a more objective view of how well things work
It means the unit does not need to take part at all
It lets the unit's managers blame the outsider for any findings
It removes the need for any written report

questions.stem: A ministry is moving its staff to a new building. Why should the OHS evaluation cover the move?
options: Moves have nothing to do with health and safety
New premises and work patterns bring new risks
Only the building contractor is responsible
The old building's risks will move with the staff

questions.stem: An evaluation finds that an agency did not report a serious injury to the authorities as the law requires. What should it recommend?
options: Wait to see whether anyone asks about the injury
Delete the record so the agency is not penalised
Report it next year with the other figures
Report it now and fix the reporting procedure

questions.stem: What should an OHS evaluation plan set out before any data are collected?
options: The findings that the executive wants to see
The names of staff to blame for incidents
The scope, criteria, methods and timetable
The budget for next year's staff party

questions.stem: Agency A had 10 injuries among 500 staff. Agency B had 15 injuries among 1,000 staff. Which statement is correct?
options: Agency B's injury rate is higher, as it had more injuries
Both agencies have the same injury rate per 100 staff
Agency A's rate is 2 per 100 staff, B's is 1.5
Agency A's rate is 1.5 per 100 staff, B's is 2

questions.stem: Which measure would best help an agency evaluate the wellbeing of its staff, alongside its injury data?
options: The number of staff parking spaces
The value of the canteen's sales
The age of the office furniture
A regular, anonymous staff wellbeing survey

questions.stem: Last year's evaluation made eight recommendations. What should this year's evaluation do first with them?
options: Ignore them, as last year is now finished
Check which were done and whether they worked
Repeat the same eight recommendations without checking
Ask the staff to forget about the old ones

questions.stem: Office staff at a tax office report neck and wrist pain. What evidence would best help the evaluation?
options: Workstation assessments and records of complaints
The total number of staff who work in each tax office
The colour scheme of the tax office's walls
The opening hours of the nearest pharmacy

questions.stem: An OHS manager has 10 minutes to present the evaluation results to the board of a public body. What is the best approach?
options: Read every figure in the 50-page report aloud
Show only the injuries that were not serious ones
Talk mainly about the history of the agency
Lead with key trends, risks and decisions needed

questions.stem: Which is NOT a good measure of an agency's OHS performance?
options: Percentage of hazard reports closed on time
Lost-time injury frequency rate
Number of safety posters printed
Results of OHS system audits

questions.stem: When reviewing a sample of incident investigation reports, what shows that an investigation was done well?
options: It finds root causes and actions that were done
It names the worker at fault and closes the file
It is filed without any recommendations
It repeats the words of the first report

questions.stem: After the evaluation's recommendations are approved, what completes the improvement cycle?
options: Filing the report and closing the matter
Carrying out actions and checking their effect
Starting a whole new evaluation the very next morning
Publishing the report in the newspapers

questions.stem: An agency has offices in Kingston, Montego Bay and Mandeville. Which scope is best for its OHS performance evaluation?
options: All sites, staff, contractors and main activities
The head office in Kingston only
Only the sites that had any accidents in the last year
Only the staff who work at desks

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names an OHS indicator, such as inspections completed, that measures action taken to prevent harm before it happens?
An agency had 4 lost-time injuries in 500,000 hours worked. What is its lost-time injury frequency rate per million hours?
What five-letter abbreviation is used for the lost-time injury frequency rate?
306 of an agency's 360 staff completed safety induction training. What percentage completed it?
What term describes the failure to report injuries and incidents, which makes OHS figures look better than they really are?
What name is usually given to the joint group of management and staff representatives that meets regularly to discuss workplace health and safety?
What one word names a systematic and independent check of whether an OHS management system meets its stated criteria?
A water utility depot had 15 recordable injuries among 1,200 workers. What is the injury rate per 100 workers?
What two-word term names the deepest underlying reason an incident happened, often found by asking 'why' several times?
What term names hazards that come from work design, workload, harassment and stress rather than from physical things?
An agency's direct injury costs were J$1,500,000, and its indirect costs were estimated at four times that amount. What was the total cost of injuries, in J$?
What term names the ranking of ways to control a hazard, from elimination at the top down to personal protective equipment?
What three-letter abbreviation names protective gear such as gloves and hearing protection, the last line of defence against a hazard?
A depot with 150 staff lost 240 days to injury in a year. What was the average number of days lost per worker?
What two-word term names the regular medical checks, such as hearing tests, for workers exposed to a health hazard at work?

essays.stem: The chief executive of a government agency with five regional offices asks you to evaluate the agency's OHS performance over the last two years. Plan how you would carry out the evaluation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first agree the purpose, scope and timetable with the chief executive: all five offices, staff and contractors, and the main activities, such as field visits, office work and vehicle use. I would set the criteria: the agency's OHS policy and objectives, the general duties of the occupational safety and health law, and good practice for similar public bodies. Next I would gather evidence from several sources: incident and near-miss reports, lost-time injuries and days lost, inspection and audit records, training records, health surveillance summaries, sickness absence and a staff survey. I would check the data are complete and recorded the same way in each office. I would consult the safety committee and interview managers and staff, and visit each office to see whether practice matches the procedures. I would then calculate indicators such as the lost-time injury frequency rate, compare trends between years and offices, benchmark with similar bodies, and find root causes of the main problems. Finally, I would write a report with findings, ranked recommendations and an action plan, present it to the executive, and agree how progress will be followed up.
markingPoints: Agrees purpose, scope and timetable
Sets clear criteria, including policy, law in general terms and good practice
Gathers evidence from several sources and checks its quality
Consults the safety committee and staff and checks practice on site
Analyses indicators, trends and causes, then reports with an action plan and follow-up

essays.stem: Compare leading and lagging indicators of OHS performance, and recommend a balanced set of indicators for a municipal corporation.
essays.modelAnswer: Lagging indicators measure harm that has already happened, such as lost-time injuries, the lost-time injury frequency rate, days lost and compensation costs. They are useful because they show the real outcome and can be compared with other bodies, but they come too late to prevent the harm, they can be distorted by under-reporting, and small numbers can rise and fall by chance. Leading indicators measure the actions that prevent harm, such as inspections completed, hazard reports closed on time, training completed and drills held. They give early warning and show whether the system is working, but they can become box-ticking if they count activity without checking quality. A balanced set is therefore best. For a municipal corporation with road, market and office staff, I would recommend: lost-time injury frequency rate and days lost per injury; the percentage of planned inspections completed; the percentage of hazard reports closed within 30 days; the percentage of staff trained for their tasks; and the results of an annual staff safety survey. Each needs a target, an owner and a clear definition, and the results should be read together.
markingPoints: Explains lagging indicators with examples
Explains leading indicators with examples
Compares the strengths and limits of each
Recommends a balanced set relevant to a municipal corporation
Says each indicator needs a target, owner and definition

essays.stem: A public utility recorded the following. Year 1: 9 lost-time injuries, 1,500,000 hours worked and 180 days lost. Year 2: 6 lost-time injuries, 1,200,000 hours worked and 210 days lost. Calculate the lost-time injury frequency rate, the severity rate (days lost per million hours) and the days lost per injury for each year, and evaluate what the figures show.
essays.modelAnswer: The frequency rate in Year 1 is 9 × 1,000,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = 6.0 lost-time injuries per million hours, and in Year 2 it is 6 × 1,000,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 5.0. The severity rate in Year 1 is 180 × 1,000,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = 120 days per million hours, and in Year 2 it is 210 × 1,000,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 175. Days lost per injury rose from 180 ÷ 9 = 20 to 210 ÷ 6 = 35. So injuries became less frequent, but each injury was more serious on average, and the total days lost went up even though fewer hours were worked. This could mean that minor injuries are no longer being reported while serious ones still are, or that a few serious incidents, such as a fall from height or a vehicle crash, drove the result. With small numbers, one serious case can change the figures a lot. I would look at the individual Year 2 cases and their causes, check reporting practice, and compare with near-miss and inspection data before concluding that performance has improved.
markingPoints: Calculates frequency rates of 6.0 and 5.0
Calculates severity rates of 120 and 175
Calculates days lost per injury of 20 and 35
Explains that frequency fell but severity rose
Suggests possible reasons, such as under-reporting or a few serious cases, and further checks

essays.stem: Explain how you would evaluate the safety culture of a large public hospital as part of an OHS performance evaluation.
essays.modelAnswer: Safety culture is the shared attitudes and habits that shape how people act on safety when no one is watching, so it cannot be measured by injury figures alone. I would use several methods. An anonymous staff survey would ask whether staff feel able to report hazards, whether managers act on reports, and whether workload allows safe practice. Interviews and small focus groups with nurses, porters, cleaners and doctors would explore the reasons behind the survey results. I would observe practice on several wards and shifts, such as safe patient handling, sharps disposal and use of protective equipment, and compare it with the procedures. Records would show how quickly hazard reports are closed and whether near misses are reported, since few near misses often means low trust rather than few problems. I would also look at how leaders behave: whether managers attend safety meetings, walk the wards and respond fairly to mistakes. I would discuss the findings with the safety committee and compare departments, then report the strengths and weaknesses with practical recommendations, such as feedback on reports and visible leadership.
markingPoints: Explains what safety culture is and why figures alone are not enough
Uses an anonymous survey and interviews or focus groups
Observes practice and checks reporting records such as near misses
Looks at leadership behaviour and responses to mistakes
Involves the safety committee and reports practical recommendations

essays.stem: Describe how you would report the findings of an OHS performance evaluation to the executive team of a ministry so that they commit to the improvements needed.
essays.modelAnswer: I would write a short report starting with an executive summary of the main findings and the decisions the executive must make. A dashboard would show the key leading and lagging indicators, with trends over two or three years, comparisons between units and a benchmark against similar bodies. I would explain the main issues in plain language, such as a rise in vehicle incidents among field officers or high stress in a call centre, with their root causes. Where possible I would show the cost of poor performance in J$, such as days lost, overtime and claims, as well as the human cost and any legal risk under the occupational safety and health law, stated in general terms. Recommendations would be ranked by risk, each with a cost, an owner and a date, so the executive can see what is needed and what it will achieve. Health data would be grouped so no person can be identified. I would present the report in person, invite the safety committee chair to speak, answer questions honestly and ask for a clear decision on each recommendation, with a date to report progress.
markingPoints: Uses an executive summary and a dashboard with trends and benchmarks
Explains issues and root causes clearly
Shows the costs, human impact and legal risk in general terms
Ranks recommendations with costs, owners and dates, protecting personal data
Presents in person, involves staff representatives and seeks decisions and follow-up

essays.stem: Evaluate the problems that can make an organisation's OHS data unreliable, and explain how an evaluator should deal with each.
essays.modelAnswer: The first problem is under-reporting. Staff may not report injuries or near misses because they fear blame, the form is hard to use or nothing happens afterwards, and targets or bonuses tied to low injury numbers make this worse. The evaluator should compare injury reports with other sources, such as first-aid records, absence data and survey answers, and recommend a no-blame reporting system and removing rewards for low numbers. A second problem is inconsistent definitions: one office may count any injury while another counts only lost-time cases. The evaluator should check the definitions, adjust the data where possible and recommend one standard form and set of categories. A third problem is missing or late data, especially from distant sites, which the evaluator should note as a limit and follow up. A fourth is small numbers: in a small unit one serious case can change the rate greatly, so trends over several years and a mix of indicators are safer than one year's rate. The evaluator should state these limits openly in the report rather than present the figures as more certain than they are.
markingPoints: Explains under-reporting and how to test and address it
Explains inconsistent definitions and how to standardise them
Identifies missing or late data and how to handle it
Explains the effect of small numbers and the need for trends and several indicators
States that limits should be reported openly

essays.stem: A public agency's evaluation shows rising stress-related absence and complaints of bullying. Explain how the evaluation should assess these psychosocial risks and what it should recommend.
essays.modelAnswer: The evaluation should treat stress and bullying as workplace hazards, just like physical ones, because they can harm health and the agency has a duty to manage them. It should first look at grouped data: absence by unit and reason, turnover, grievances, employee assistance programme use and exit interview themes, keeping individual cases confidential. An anonymous survey can measure workload, control over work, support from managers, relationships and clarity of roles. Focus groups, run by someone trusted and independent, can explore the causes in more depth. The evaluator should review whether the agency has a policy on respect at work and a fair complaints procedure, and whether managers are trained to use them. From this, the evaluation can identify where risks are highest and why, such as staff shortages in one unit or a manager's behaviour. Recommendations might include adjusting workloads and staffing, training managers, reinforcing the anti-bullying policy and complaints route, promoting the employee assistance programme, and adding a wellbeing measure to the agency's OHS indicators, with a follow-up survey to check whether things improve.
markingPoints: Treats stress and bullying as workplace hazards to be managed
Uses grouped data and keeps individual cases confidential
Uses an anonymous survey and independent focus groups to find causes
Reviews the policy, complaints procedure and manager training
Recommends practical controls and a way to measure improvement

essays.stem: A municipal corporation uses contractors for drain cleaning, road patching and building repairs. Explain how its OHS evaluation should assess the safety performance of these contractors and the council's own control of them.
essays.modelAnswer: The council keeps duties for work done on its behalf, so the evaluation must cover contractors. It should first check how contractors are chosen: whether tenders ask for safety records, method statements and evidence of training, and whether these are scored, not just filed. It should review contract terms to see that safety requirements, reporting of incidents and the right to stop unsafe work are written in. Next it should look at how the council manages contractors once work starts: site inductions, permits for high-risk work such as confined spaces in drains, and supervision visits with recorded findings. The evaluator should gather contractors' incident and near-miss figures, compare them with the council's own staff and look for patterns, such as injuries during road patching from passing traffic. Visiting a sample of work sites would show whether practice matches the paperwork. The evaluation should then judge whether the council's controls are working and recommend improvements, such as better scoring of safety in tenders, regular contractor review meetings and removing contractors with poor records from future lists.
markingPoints: Explains that the council keeps duties for contracted work
Assesses selection, tender scoring and contract terms
Assesses induction, permits and supervision during the work
Gathers contractor incident data and checks practice on site
Judges the controls and recommends improvements

essays.stem: Explain how an OHS performance evaluation can check whether an organisation is meeting its general duties under the occupational safety and health law, without becoming a simple checklist of rules.
essays.modelAnswer: In general terms, the law expects an employer to provide a safe workplace, assess and control risks, give information, training and supervision, consult workers, provide welfare facilities, prepare for emergencies and report serious incidents. The evaluation can use these duties as headings, but for each it should ask whether the arrangements actually work, not just whether a document exists. For risk assessment, it should sample assessments and check on site that the controls are in place and used. For training, it should test whether staff can explain safe methods, not only count certificates. For consultation, it should check whether the safety committee meets, whether its concerns are acted on and whether staff know their representatives. For emergencies, drill records and timings show effectiveness. For reporting, it should compare incident records with absence and first-aid data. Combining document review, observation, interviews and data in this way gives a judgement on how well the duties are met in practice. Where the law's requirements are unclear, the evaluator should seek advice rather than guess, and the report should state any gaps plainly.
markingPoints: Outlines the employer's general duties without quoting sections
Uses the duties as headings but tests whether arrangements work
Gives examples of checking practice, such as training or drills
Combines documents, observation, interviews and data
Seeks advice where unclear and reports gaps plainly

essays.stem: Your OHS evaluation of a ministry has produced ten findings. Explain how you would turn them into an improvement action plan and make sure the plan is carried out.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first rank the findings by risk, using the likely harm and how often it could happen, and by any legal duty involved, so that the most serious issues, such as vehicle incidents among field staff, come first. For each finding I would write a clear action that deals with the root cause, preferring controls high in the hierarchy, such as changing the work or equipment, over training or PPE alone. Each action would have an owner at the right level, a realistic date, an estimated cost in J$ and a measure of success, such as fewer incidents or hazard reports closed on time. I would agree the plan with the safety committee and managers, and get the executive's approval and budget. Quick, low-cost actions can start at once while larger ones are scheduled. Progress would be tracked on a simple register reviewed at each safety committee meeting and reported to the executive every quarter, with overdue actions explained. Finally, at the next evaluation I would check not only whether actions were completed but whether they improved performance, and adjust the plan if they did not.
markingPoints: Ranks findings by risk and legal duty
Writes actions that address root causes, using the hierarchy of control
Gives each action an owner, date, cost and measure
Gets agreement, approval and budget
Tracks progress regularly and checks whether actions worked

practical1.title: Evaluate an agency's OHS performance from its records
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up data pack for a public body, such as a municipal corporation or a government agency with three sites. It includes two years of incident and near-miss records, hours worked, days lost, inspection and training records, sickness absence, a staff survey summary, the OHS policy and the safety committee minutes. As a group, evaluate the body's OHS performance and write a short evaluation report. Each member has a named role: data analyst (builds a spreadsheet and calculates the lost-time injury frequency rate, severity rate, days lost per injury and injury rate per 100 workers for each year and site, checking every figure twice); indicators analyst (calculates leading indicators, such as inspections completed and hazard reports closed on time, and draws trend charts); systems reviewer (reviews the policy, procedures and committee minutes against the general duties of the occupational safety and health law and notes gaps); culture and wellbeing analyst (analyses the survey and absence data, keeping all health information grouped and anonymous); and report writer (writes the executive summary, findings and ranked recommendations). In a group of four, the report writer also carries out the systems review. Every member writes the section for their role.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet and word processing software
Evaluation report and action plan templates
Printer, paper, flipchart paper and markers
photos: The spreadsheet on screen with the calculated rates for each year and site
The trend charts of leading and lagging indicators
The systems review notes with gaps marked
The survey and absence analysis, showing grouped data only
The finished report, open at the findings and ranked recommendations
checklist: Took a named role and completed their section of the report
Rates are calculated correctly with the right formulas and were checked twice
Leading and lagging indicators are both used and read together
Gaps against policy and general legal duties are identified without quoting sections
Health and absence data are grouped so no person can be identified
Findings identify likely root causes and data limits, such as under-reporting
Recommendations are ranked by risk and are practical
safety: Treat the data pack as confidential; return all papers to the assessor
Keep all health information grouped and anonymous, as the data protection law requires in general
Respect each member's analysis and share the workload fairly
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Present an OHS evaluation and agree an action plan
practical2.brief: Using a made-up OHS evaluation summary from the assessor (or the report from Practical 1), your group holds a 40-minute joint meeting of the executive team and the safety committee of a public body, then writes up the results. Each member has a named role: chief executive (chairs the meeting, keeps time and makes sure decisions are reached); OHS manager (presents the main findings in no more than six slides and proposes the ranked recommendations); staff safety representative (raises staff concerns from a role card and tests whether the actions are practical); finance and human resources director (comments on the costs in J$, the staffing effects and how the actions will be funded); and secretary (records the minutes, decisions and actions). In a group of four, the chief executive also takes the minutes with help from the finance director. The meeting must agree at least six actions, each with an owner, date, cost and measure of success. After the meeting, the group writes the minutes, a one-page action plan and a short notice to all staff explaining what was found and what will change. Every member writes or checks part of these documents.
materials: Evaluation summary and role cards from the assessor
Computer and screen for the slides
Minutes, action plan and staff notice templates
photos: The meeting in progress (faces only if all agree)
The recommendations ranked on a flipchart or slide during the meeting
The action plan and the staff notice
checklist: Took a named role and prepared for it
The presentation leads with key trends, risks and decisions needed
Staff concerns were raised and answered respectfully
Each agreed action has an owner, date, cost and measure of success
Actions favour controls high in the hierarchy of control
The staff notice is clear, accurate and identifies no individual
safety: Keep the evaluation summary and minutes confidential; return all papers to the assessor
Do not name or describe any real person's injury or health
Keep the meeting respectful: challenge ideas, not people
Share the writing fairly and take a short break after the meeting
